t.1.33.1: O Rāghava, when that Brahmadatta had completed the marriage and departed, the sonless king arranged a sacrifice meant to bring forth a son, so that he might obtain a son.
t.1.33.2: While the sacrifice was in progress, Kuśa, the son of Brahmā, supremely pleased, then spoke to King Kuśanābha.
t.1.33.3: O son, a most righteous son equal to you will be born to you. You will obtain Gādhi, and through him you will win everlasting fame in the world.
t.1.33.4: Having spoken thus to King Kuśanābha, O Rāma, Kuśa entered the sky and went to the eternal world of Brahmā.
t.1.33.5: Then, after some time, to the wise Kuśanābha was born a son supremely devoted to dharma, Gādhi by name.
t.1.33.6: That supremely righteous Gādhi is my father, O Kākutstha; born in the lineage of Kuśa, I am Kauśika, O Raghunandana.
t.1.33.7: And I also had an elder sister, O Rāghava, devoted to her vows, Satyavatī by name, who was given in marriage to Ṛcīka.
t.1.33.8: Following her husband, she went to heaven in her own body; that most noble one, Kauśikī, then flowed forth as a great river.
t.1.33.9: My sister, divine, delightful and of holy waters, has taken refuge on Himavant and flowed forth out of a wish for the welfare of the world.
t.1.33.10: Therefore I dwell happily on the slope of Himavant, self-restrained, bound by affection for my sister Kauśikī, O Raghunandana.
t.1.33.11: That holy Satyavatī, firmly established in truth and righteousness, devoted to her husband and greatly blessed, is Kauśikī, the best of rivers.
t.1.33.12: For I, Rāma, left her because of my vow and came here; having reached the Siddhāśrama, I have attained success through your power.
t.1.33.13: This, O Rāma, is the origin of my own lineage and of this land, now recounted, O mighty-armed one, since you have asked me about it.
t.1.33.14: Half the night has passed, O Kākutstha, while I have been telling these tales. Go to sleep, may good fortune be yours, so that there may be no hindrance to our journey here.
t.1.33.15: All the trees are motionless, the beasts and birds have settled into hiding, and the directions are pervaded by the darkness of night, O Raghunandana.
t.1.33.16: Slowly the twilight is parting away; the sky, covered as if with eyes, dense with constellations and stars, shines with its lights.
t.1.33.17: And the cool-rayed moon, the hare-marked one who dispels the darkness of the world, is rising, O lord, gladdening with its radiance the minds of living beings in the world.
t.1.33.18: All the creatures of the night roam about here and there, and so do the hosts of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, fierce and feeding on raw flesh.
t.1.33.19: Having spoken thus, the greatly radiant great sage fell silent. All the sages honored him, saying, "Well said, well said!"
t.1.33.20: Rāma too, together with Saumitri, somewhat filled with wonder, praised the tiger among sages and then betook himself to sleep.
